name: Rafael Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, 43, and I lead the difficult home and business electrical repairs with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. I'm among the strongest at finding a fault and checking the crew's work, but I work for the firm rather than own it. My pay is high for the trade, my partner Casey maintains museum displays, and we've children aged twelve and sixteen, a mortgage and twelve months of expenses saved, with plenty of electrical firms nearby. I use approved AI daily for checked job notes and finding reference pages; I enjoy a new tool that exposes my wrong first guess, but dislike a sales demonstration that hides the mistakes behind a fast answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful tool doesn't owe us a dramatic story. If it helps find the right old job note, we'll use it and still check what happened on site. I'd rather get the repair right than be the person who sounded most excited in the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and the household money feel secure here. Our regular wages cover the mortgage and family costs, and a year's expenses saved gives us real room. Plenty of local firms do similar work, but I don't need another employer to rescue next month's payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the difficult repairs and checking the crew's work now and through the next year. I'd continue using my daily tools with the original readings and approved references beside them. I'd keep our normal budget and the existing cash reserve, rather than turn an ordinary year into a reason to buy another subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and happy to enjoy a small improvement without needing it to change my identity. I can leave the phone alone after work. The children don't need a new technology briefing over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when your first fault diagnosis was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down the first guess, what test changed it and the actual result. I don't mind an apprentice seeing that I changed my mind. Being the lead shouldn't mean making the first guess impossible to question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you think about the existing reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it separate from the wages we use each month. Twelve months gives us choices in a quiet spell, but it isn't the rest of a working life. Maintaining the cash we already have isn't a new deposit.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** without making them perform a dramatic story about the whole trade.
I'd value **the correct repair** more than sounding excited at a meeting.
think: Our wages and **twelve-month reserve** make current mortgage and family costs feel secure.
Plentiful **nearby employers** provide options without becoming a necessary rescue for next month's payment.
do: Keep **repair leadership** and crew checks through the next year.
Continue daily tools with **original readings** and approved references, retaining the normal budget and existing reserve.
feel: **Calm and interested**, able to enjoy a small improvement and leave family dinners free of technology briefings.
S0.quote: Being the lead shouldn't mean making the first guess impossible to question.
fieldNote: His **secure baseline** follows high pay, covering wages and a substantial reserve rather than a belief that technical standing prevents all change.
Daily **AI checks** and existing cash remain ordinary continuity, with no new-learning or increased-saving tag invented.

steps.text: Keep leading difficult repairs with checked daily tools and the ordinary household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the people doing the work should help decide what happens to the saved time. I'd offer to test the new AI drawing-comparison feature, which compares a parts order with the job drawing, but show the errors as well as the speed. I'd ask the staff association for a joint discussion before office savings became staffing decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own physical repair hours and Casey's practical display work look secure over the next few years. I'm uneasy about the office staff having decisions made around them while the site crew congratulates itself. I'd rather use my own room to experiment to make the discussion more honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request a six-job trial of the new comparison feature only free during paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours maintained. I'd check every suggested discrepancy against the original drawing and actual parts before it entered a live order. During the first year I'd help the association collect staff questions and seek a written meeting response about hours and paid learning, keeping my existing repair role while proposals remained unagreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the gains are shared, and interested in what the trial might teach me. I don't need to defend a bad suggestion because I offered to test it. I'd want the office staff in the room when we read the results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the feature invented a discrepancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the trial and show the original evidence beside the invented item. I wouldn't let a neat comparison override the actual order or licence responsibilities. A tool earns another try by exposing a mistake, not by asking me to hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the meeting was friendly but gave no clear terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd ask what was actually agreed about hours and learning, and request the answer in writing. I'd keep the current paid arrangement until there was a real change. A pleasant meeting isn't a second set of paid hours.

I'd test **AI comparison errors** openly instead of show only the speed of a new feature.
think: Our **near-term physical wages** look secure while office staff face more immediate thinking-task changes.
I'm uneasy about **unshared decisions**, with financial room to test the tool and ask specific questions.

Seek a **written staff response** on hours and paid learning through the association, retaining current paid repairs until terms change.
feel: **Uneasy and curious**, willing to reject a bad tool result and include office staff when reviewing the evidence.

fieldNote: The **new comparison feature** is genuinely distinct learning, while his existing daily note and reference tools remain routine work.
The **trial conditions** preserve free access, paid shifts, weekly wages and hours; a staff discussion does not become an assumed agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association thinking AGI comes in 2028 and capable robots follow around 2031 for physical work. We need notice and paid learning before people lose hours, not a lecture afterwards. I'd still use the tools, but I wouldn't call my own master electrician's licence a guarantee for everyone at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair hours could shrink when capable robots spread, and Casey's physical work could change too. Our year's reserve gives choices, not a lifetime wage. I'd be anxious about both jobs changing, while still able to make a small affordable experiment instead of a desperate bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask Casey to agree a limit of 40 monthly from future wages for a broad share fund, meaning small holdings across many companies, only after essentials and known fees were covered while the twelve-month cash reserve stayed intact. I'd make no purchase until we agreed those terms, and stop if wages no longer left the surplus. In 2029 I'd keep paid repairs and help the association seek staffing notice and paid transition learning, counting neither a hoped-for investment return nor an unsigned staff proposal as household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with enough room to choose a small risk rather than pretend I can avoid every risk. I might lose the invested money. Forty a month is a limit on the experiment, not a prediction about what the machines will earn us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the share purchase from becoming imaginary income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the purchase statements and full fees beside the household budget, without counting a rise before selling anything. A broad fund can still lose money. If the surplus vanished, the purchases would stop before we borrowed or touched the cash reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek shared terms if you also want a private investment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my small private investment isn't a substitute for wages, notice or paid learning. I'd still ask for collective terms for people who couldn't afford even forty. Owning a small piece of companies doesn't give the crew a guaranteed paid Friday.

I'd seek **notice and paid learning** before workers lose hours, without treating my licence as a collective guarantee.
think: Both physical household jobs could lose **hours later**, including my own repair work.
Our **year's reserve** offers choices without becoming a lifelong wage or eliminating the risk in a small experiment.
do: Invest at most **40 monthly** from future wages only after essentials and known fees, with Casey agreeing and the reserve intact.
Stop purchases before **borrowing or reserve use** if wages leave no surplus, counting no hoped-for return as income.
Keep **2029 paid repairs** while seeking notice and paid transition learning through the association, assuming no unsigned agreement.
feel: **Anxious with choices**, accepting that the small investment could lose money without making it the household's wage plan.
S2.quote: Owning a small piece of companies doesn't give the crew a guaranteed paid Friday.
fieldNote: His **investment decision** is an affordable conditional experiment, not a return forecast or a claim that shares replace wages after automation.
Future **wage surplus** funds purchases only after essentials and known fees, with partner agreement and the full twelve-month reserve protected.

Protect twelve-month cash reserve; stop purchases before borrowing or reserve use if wages leave no surplus

Seek actual signed staffing notice and paid-learning terms through the association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test a small decision and stop if it doesn't fit, rather than buy a whole new future. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd still ask for shared paid-learning terms now, not use the extra time to make preparation a private bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present repair and display wages look secure over the next few years, with room to review what really changes. I'm uneasy about later physical hours, but not expecting an immediate household wage loss in this picture. I'd use the extra time for checked choices rather than assume a new label made me safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the same capped share purchases now only from future wage surplus after essentials and known fees, with Casey agreeing and the twelve-month cash reserve intact. We'd review the actual contributions and fees quarterly, stopping before borrowing or reserve use if there was no surplus and counting no hoped-for return as income. In 2032 I'd keep paid repairs and pursue notice and paid learning with the association, asking what terms were actually signed before calling any protection won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with time to revise rather than defend the first choice. I'd rather close a small experiment honestly than keep feeding it because I once sounded enthusiastic. The reserve should give us room to decide, not an excuse to stop reading the statements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the share fund lost value while wages still held?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the loss in the household account and ask whether the next 40 was still something we could afford to risk. We could stop even if wages still covered essentials. My 40 monthly share purchase limit isn't a promise to keep buying after a bad result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What family commitments would you check in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032 our children would be eighteen and twenty-two, so we'd check actual household commitments rather than invent school pickups. I wouldn't use their possible wages as our investment fund or our mortgage plan. Their next choices need a conversation, not an entry I make in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends a decade gives us several chances to revise the plan rather than ten years of being told to reinvent ourselves. I'd still ask the association to make paid learning and staffing notice concrete. I want our children to see questions being checked, not adults performing certainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current work and household money look secure over the next few years, and I like the room to try modest changes. I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. The later question stays with me, but it doesn't make today's mortgage feel unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the share experiment at a maximum 40 monthly from future wage surplus only after essentials and known fees, with Casey agreeing and the twelve-month reserve intact. We'd review contributions and fees quarterly, stopping before borrowing or reserve use if no surplus remained and counting no hoped-for return as income. In 2037 I'd keep paid repairs and help the association check actual staffing notice and paid-learning terms, bringing household reviews forward if wages weakened earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own near-term position, and interested in what I can learn without betting the household. I still can't promise the same job at 56. I can enjoy the coming weekend while keeping an actual review date in the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would household responsibilities mean with adult children in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be twenty-three and twenty-seven in 2037, so we'd ask what was actually needed and agreed. I'd neither keep today's school duties in the plan nor assume adults could never need help. Their possible wages aren't my solution to the later mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the association never secured the requested terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid arrangement we actually had and show colleagues which requests were still outstanding. Repeating a proposal for years doesn't turn it into a contract. My private experiment wouldn't give the employer permission to stop discussing other workers' paid time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both our physical wages could change around 2031 before we'd checked many real alternatives. Paid learning, staffing notice and staff involved before the decisions would help more than being told to make a private financial bet. My little share purchase isn't a replacement for a fair paid week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether enjoying new tools makes it hard to admit a bad experiment. Sometimes it does, which is why I want the actual errors and costs in view. I'd rather have the apprentice see me stop a weak idea than see me hide behind a confident explanation.

headlineQuote: My little share purchase isn't a replacement for a fair paid week.
portrait: Rafael, **43**, leads repairs with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, and is among the firm's strongest fault finders.
He has **higher pay**, twelve months saved, plentiful local employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with museum-display technician partner Casey.
He uses **AI daily**, checking real work and testing new features only free within paid shifts with normal wages and hours maintained.
His **small share experiment** uses capped future wage surplus after essentials and fees, with partner consent, protected cash and no promised return.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time to check alternatives before capable robots could change both physical household wages around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid learning**, staffing notice and worker involvement before decisions would help more than expecting private investments to replace fair wages.
